response.text:
I'll work through the drafts systematically, applying each test and the gate test, while excluding residues of authorized cuts.

---

**Candidate 1 — Ch 005, draft passage:**
> "The effect was deepened by the official ceremony which afterwards took place in Faneuil Hall, where the boy was taken to hear his uncle deliver a Eulogy."

**Source has:** "…the boy was taken to hear his uncle, Edward Everett, deliver a Eulogy. Like all Mr. Everett's orations, it was an admirable piece of oratory…"

The uncle is named "Edward Everett" in the source. Edward Everett is on the authorized-removal list, so the elision of his name is an authorized cut. The draft says "his uncle" — the reader already knows from Ch 004 draft that this is the Adams family, and Ch 005 draft para 1 mentions "Abigail Brown … married … to Charles Francis Adams" but does not name any uncle. However, Ch 004 source (and draft) does refer to "his uncle, the minister of the First Church" in the very first paragraph. That uncle is a different person (the Frothingham uncle). Neither uncle has been identified as the Faneuil Hall orator in the draft. Still — Edward Everett is an authorized removal, so a dangling "his uncle" here is a *direct residue* of that authorized cut. **Not a valid finding.**

---

**Candidate 2 — Ch 005, draft passage:**
> "The critics called him cold. No doubt, such perfect poise was not maintained by nature without a sacrifice of the qualities which would have upset it."

**Source has:** "The same thing might perhaps have been said of John Quincy Adams, but in him his associates averred that it was accompanied by mental restlessness and often by lamentable want of judgment. No one ever charged Charles Francis Adams with this fault. The critics charged him with just the opposite defect. They called him cold."

The source's "They called him cold" is the *conclusion* of a two-sided contrast: John Quincy Adams was charged with want of judgment → Charles Francis was charged with the *opposite* (coldness). The draft cuts the first side entirely. The draft's "The critics called him cold" arrives with no preceding contrast; the reader has just read praise of his perfect poise, so "called him cold" still follows logically as a dissenting view on that poise. The sentence parses and the logic holds without the JQA comparison. The connective is not a pivot word ("but," "however") — it is simply an abrupt assertion. A competent reader understands: people criticized his poise as coldness. They are reading a less-ornamented version, not a confused one. **Not a valid finding.**

---

**Candidate 3 — Ch 005, draft passage:**
> "Had it been less balanced, he would have gone with Garrison and Wendell Phillips into secession."

**Source has:** "Had it been less balanced than it was, he would have gone with Mr. Garrison, Mr. Wendell Phillips, Mr. Edmund Quincy, and Theodore Parker, into secession."

Minor-character compression only. Still parses. **Not a valid finding.**

---

**Candidate 4 — Ch 005, draft passage:**
> "In that respect, and in that only, Charles Sumner was like him…" — this sentence is **entirely cut** from the draft. The draft moves directly from "his mind was aristocratic to the tenth generation" into the Sumner paragraph beginning "Sumner, in almost every other quality, was different from his associates—altogether out of line."

The source's transition sentence was: "In that respect, and in that only, Charles Sumner was like him, but Sumner, in almost every other quality, was quite different from his three associates—altogether out of line."

The draft renders this as: "Of the four men, Dana was the most marked. Disguise it as he liked, his mind was aristocratic to the tenth generation. [¶] Sumner, in almost every other quality, was different from his associates—altogether out of line."

The draft's Sumner paragraph opens with "in almost every other quality, was different" — different *from whom*? The antecedent of the implicit comparison in "almost every other quality" was Dana (the "that respect" = Dana's aristocratic quality). Without the source's bridge sentence, does a reader know what quality Sumner *shared*? The draft sentence "Sumner, in almost every other quality, was different from his associates" is grammatically self-contained — it just says he differed from his associates. It does *not* say "in that respect … like him." So the reader is not told what Sumner *did* share with Dana. But does this cause genuine confusion? The draft sentence still asserts Sumner was different from his associates generally; a reader is not misled, just denied a nuance. The gate test: the reader understands Sumner was distinctive; the specific shared trait (aristocratic feeling) is lost but no false impression is created. **Not a valid finding** (less ornamented, not broken).

---

**Candidate 5 — Ch 005, draft passage:**
> "The standards of Boston were high, much affected by the old clerical self-respect…" — This entire paragraph is **cut** from the draft.

No residual seam remains in the draft. **Not applicable.**

---

**Candidate 6 — Ch 005, draft passage:**
> "Mr. Adams was a younger man, greatly biassed by his father, and by the inherited feud between Quincy and State Street; but personal relations were friendly as far as a boy could see, and the innumerable cousins went regularly to the First Church every Sunday in winter, and slept through their uncle's sermons."

**Source has:** "Neither of them had much in common with Mr. Adams … but personal relations were friendly … and the innumerable cousins went regularly to the First Church every Sunday in winter, and slept through their uncle's sermons, without once thinking to ask what the sermons were supposed to mean for them."

"Neither of them" in the source refers to Edward Everett and Dr. Frothingham. Both are authorized removals. The draft's version strips the referent of "their uncle's sermons" — whose uncle? The draft's preceding sentence mentions Charles Francis Adams and Abigail Brown's children, but does not name any uncle who preaches. In Ch 004 draft the uncle who christened Henry was "the minister of the First Church." That minister is Dr. Frothingham — an authorized removal. So: "their uncle's sermons" has no antecedent uncle established anywhere in the Ch 005 draft (the Ch 004 draft identifies only an unnamed "uncle, the minister of the First Church"). A reader of only the draft would not know which uncle preaches; "their uncle" dangles. But — this is a *direct residue of the authorized cut* of Dr. Frothingham. **Not a valid finding** (authorized removal).

---

**Candidate 7 — Ch 004, draft passage:**
> "He divined his great-grandfather's character from his own; never for a moment did he connect the two ideas of Boston and John Adams; they were separate and antagonistic; the idea of John Adams went with Quincy."

**Source has:** "He knew as yet nothing about his great-grandfather, who had died a dozen years before his own birth: he took for granted that any great-grandfather of his must have always been good, and his enemies wicked; but he divined his great-grandfather's character from his own."

The draft cuts the source's setup ("He knew as yet nothing about his great-grandfather … he took for granted …") and begins directly with "He divined his great-grandfather's character from his own." The reader has not been told the boy knew nothing about John Adams and was reasoning by analogy; instead the draft asserts he *divined* the character. Does this confuse? The sentence is grammatically complete and the referent "his great-grandfather" is inferrable from the preceding draft context (John Adams has been mentioned). No logical pivot word is broken. The reader understands the claim without the setup, even if the reasoning is less explained. **Not a valid finding.**

---

**Candidate 8 — Ch 005, draft passage:**
> "The discussions were always serious; the Free Soil Party took itself quite seriously; and they were habitual because Mr. Adams had undertaken to edit a newspaper as the organ of these gentlemen."

**Source has:** "…who came to discuss its policy and expression."

The draft cuts "who came to discuss its policy and expression" — a relative clause. The matrix clause still parses. Explicit rejection rule applies. **Not a valid finding.**

---

**Candidate 9 — Ch 005, draft passage:**
> "Palfrey was the oldest, and often the most agreeable, for his talk was lighter and his range wider; he had wit, and the give-and-take of dinner-table exchange."

Source glosses Palfrey as someone "Born to be a man of the world, he forced himself to be clergyman, professor, or statesman, while, like every other true Bostonian, he yearned for the ease of the Athenæum Club in Pall Mall…" This is a definitional/characterizing gloss. Without it, "Palfrey was the oldest, and often the most agreeable" still stands on its own; the reader simply has less context about Palfrey's inner tension. Explicit rejection rule (explanatory relative/characterizing clause cut; matrix clause still conveys the meaning). **Not a valid finding.**

---

**Candidate 10 — Ch 005, draft passage:**
> "Dana affected to be still before the mast, a direct, bluff, vigorous seaman, and only as one got to know him better did one find the man of excessive refinement trying to work like a day-laborer, as though he were still carrying hides at Monterey. Of the four men, Dana was the most marked. Disguise it as he liked, his mind was aristocratic to the tenth generation."

Source: "…but he might have said what his lifelong friend William M. Evarts used to say: 'I pride myself on my success in doing not the things I like to do, but the things I don't like to do.' Dana's ideal of life was to be a great Englishman, with a seat on the front benches of the House of Commons until he should be promoted to the woolsack…"

All cut. But the draft's condensed sentences remain self-standing. No broken pivot, no dangling pronoun. **Not a valid finding.**

---

**Candidate 11 — Ch 005, draft passage:**
> "The boy got as little education, fitting him for his own time, from the one as from the other."

**Source has:** "The boy got as little education, fitting him for his own time, from the one as from the other, and he got no more from his contact with the gentlemen themselves who were all types of the past."

The source's full sentence has two parallel "got … from" clauses: (1) from the newspapers/proof-reading and (2) from contact with the gentlemen. The draft cuts the second clause. The remaining clause "from the one as from the other" compares two things: "the one" = proof-reading/Novanglus texts, "the other" = the Boston Whig discussions. In the draft, has "the other" been established? The draft says: "At the same time Mr. Adams was editing the 'Works' of his grandfather John Adams, and made the boy read texts for proof-correction. The boy got as little education, fitting him for his own time, from the one as from the other." Yes — "the one" and "the other" refer to the proof-correction work and the anti-slavery discussions, both mentioned in the immediately preceding draft sentences. The sentence parses cleanly. **Not a valid finding.**

---

**Candidate 12 — Ch 004, draft passage:**
> "The funeral service in the Quincy church, with its surroundings of national respect and family pride, left an overwhelming impression on the boy's mind."

**Source has:** "Many a boy might be ruined by much less than the emotions of the funeral service in the Quincy church … By another dramatic chance it happened that the clergyman of the parish, Dr. Lunt, was an unusual pulpit orator … His extraordinarily refined appearance, his dignity of manner, his deeply cadenced voice, his remarkable English and his fine appreciation, gave to the funeral service a character that left an overwhelming impression on the boy's mind."

Dr. Lunt is an authorized removal. The source attributes the overwhelming impression *specifically to Dr. Lunt's oratory*. The draft strips the cause and states simply that the service "left an overwhelming impression." The reader understands the event without the source's explanation of *why* it was impressive. Explicit rejection rule: "A detail's cause or origin is cut; the reader understands the event without the source's flourish." Also this is a direct residue of the Dr. Lunt authorized removal. **Not a valid finding.**

---

**Candidate 13 — Ch 004, draft passage:**
> "The effect was deepened by the official ceremony which afterwards took place in Faneuil Hall, where the boy was taken to hear his uncle deliver a Eulogy. Already the boy knew that the dead President could not be in it, and had even learned why he would have been out of place there; for knowledge was beginning to come fast."

The source explains *why* the President would be out of place through the extended passage about Edward Everett's oration and the Adamses' quarrel with State Street. The draft then proceeds directly: "The shadow of the War of 1812 still hung over State Street…" The "why" the President would be out of place is actually answered by what follows in the draft (the inherited quarrel with State Street, Hartford Convention, etc.), so the reader can follow. **Not a valid finding.**

---

**Candidate 14 — Ch 005, draft passage:**
> "Even the violent reaction after 1848, and the return of all Europe to military practices, never for a moment shook the true faith. No one, except Karl Marx, foresaw radical change."

This is compressed from source but grammatically intact with no broken pivot. **Not a valid finding.**

---

**Candidate 15 — Ch 005, draft, opening paragraph:**

> "Among his seven children was Abigail Brown, married September 3, 1829, to Charles Francis Adams."

Source: lists all seven children with names. Draft cuts to only Abigail. The other children including Edward Everett's wife Charlotte are authorized removals (Edward Everett is on the list). No structural damage; the sentence stands. **Not a valid finding.**

---

After exhaustive review of all candidates against all six tests and the gate test, **no passage in either draft chapter fails the structural coherence tests** in a way that would genuinely confuse a competent reader who has not seen the source. Every compression that produces a potential seam either (a) leaves the remaining sentence fully parseable with available antecedents, (b) is a direct residue of an authorized cut, or (c) merely removes ornamentation while leaving the logical and referential structure intact.
